title: His family carried the dead cattle
hookLine: Ravidas sings that his family carried dead animals near Benares, yet great men bow to him now (Malar, Ravidas, ang 1293)

lines: JOBS WE KNOW BY THEIR ABSENCE.
cards: Before dawn, a truck stops outside, and someone you'll never meet carries off your trash. A worker in a hospital basement washes what nobody wants to wash.
Somewhere, a person handles the dead so the rest of us don't have to. These jobs get noticed mostly by their absence, the day they aren't done.
In Raag Malar, Ravidas opens a hymn by addressing the whole town and naming his family's work. Not hinting at it. Naming it.

teach.h: PEOPLE OF THE TOWN, MY CASTE IS KNOWN.
teach.b: Two hymns sit side by side on Ang 1293 of the Guru Granth Sahib. Four days ago this path heard the second, with the learned bowing. Today, start with the first.
It opens, in paraphrase: people of the town, my caste is well known; it is the leather-workers' caste. And in my heart I hold the Lord's virtues. Then a picture from a scribe's desk.
The palm tree is counted impure, and so is the paper made from its leaves.

teach.h: PALM-LEAF PAPER, BOWED TO WHEN IT HOLDS PRAISE.
teach.b: But when the Lord's praise is written on that paper, people bow before it and worship it. The material doesn't change. What's written on it changes how it's treated.
Ravidas sets himself right there: the same family, the same trade, and the Name written into him. The second hymn adds one small word that carries a lot: still.

teach.h: STILL HAULING DEAD CATTLE IN BENARES.
teach.b: His relatives, he says, still go around Benares hauling away dead cattle. He doesn't say they used to, or that he got out, so the honor can't be explained by escape.
Brahmins of careful conduct bow before him anyway, and he calls himself the servant of the Lord's servants. In that same hymn he names Kabir too, as if to say: the Lord keeps doing this.

He doesn't ask to be reclassified, or call the work beneath him. Sikh teaching has a name for honest work: kirat karni, earning by your own labor. So today's line, every job is holy, isn't Ravidas's exact phrase.
It's what his song does: it names a job the town shrank from, right at the top, and doesn't apologize.

how: Sikhs hear these hymns of Ravidas in the gurdwara as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and the Sikh ideal of kirat karni, honest work, honors labor of every kind.

o: the prayer said before starting a job
earning a living by honest work of your own
giving a tenth of your income to charity

games.q: inside the hymn — tap the pairs.

s: the palm-leaf paper becomes a different material when praise is written on it
it stays the same leaf; what's written on it changes how people treat it.
in the hymn, learned Brahmins bow before Ravidas while his family still hauls cattle
both stand in one hymn: his relatives still haul dead cattle around Benares, and Brahmins of careful conduct bow.
'every job is holy' is Ravidas's exact phrase
it's today's line for what the hymn does, not a quotation.

games.q: you're Ravidas, singing to a town that knows exactly where your family comes from. how do you begin?
o: say nothing about family; sing only of God.
name your caste and your family's work out loud.
games.why: he names it: people of the town, my caste is well known. then he sets the learned bowing right beside the dead cattle.

practice: Trace something you touched today back to the hands that dealt with its mess: the drain, the bin, the floor, the laundry, the shoes.
Let one of those workers come to mind, even without a face, and stay with them a few breaths, without pity, the way Ravidas stays with his family's work. Waheguru on each breath out, if you pray.

wordCard.voice: Kirat karni. Sikh teaching's name for earning by your own labor: Ravidas naming his family's trade before the whole town, and not apologizing for it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: people of the town, the words that open Ravidas's first Malar hymn (Ang 1293).

carryVoice: Your line: every job is holy. Someone's hard work is holding up your day. See you tomorrow.
